payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Turn the image into a drawing made from chalk
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly render its surfaces with a chalk-like appearance, rather than merely adding grain or a filter to the source image?
node.criteria: Pass if, compared with the source, visible surface marks or tonal treatment make the image read as rendered with chalk. Fail if the source’s surface appearance remains or the only change is generic grain or filtering that does not produce a chalk-like rendering. Unknown only if the surface treatment cannot be observed.
node.endpoint: The drawing has visibly chalk-like surface marks or tonal treatment.
node.necessity: The instruction specifies that the drawing is made from chalk; a drawing without a visibly chalk-like rendering does not fulfill that requested material appearance.

node_traces.evidence: Compared with the source photograph, the edited image has broad, visibly smudged tonal strokes across the sky, ground, and foliage, with softened chalk-like shading around the giraffes rather than just added uniform grain. These surface treatments make the scene read as a chalk drawing.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s criterion is broadly aligned with the requested chalk rendering, and its evidence cites visible smudged strokes and softened shading. However, the trace’s confident “pass” conflicts with the aggregate reference of “partial”; that mismatch is not proof that the chalk treatment is absent. Clarify how to distinguish partial material treatment from a scene that consistently reads as a chalk drawing, while retaining the explicit exclusion of generic grain/filtering alone. Keep the source-versus-edit comparison and require evidence across the image rather than relying on a few smudged regions. Investigate the yes-versus-partial aggregation or label mapping separately: the trace is valid, queried, and dependency-free, so there is no indicated transport or schema failure, and low confidence or repeated variation should not be used as evidence that the requested edit is missing."}
